records.text: Skjöldr was the name of a son of Óðinn, from whom the Skjöldungar are descended. He had his seat and ruled the lands that are now called Danmörk, but were then called Gotland. Skjöldr had a son called Friðleifr, who ruled the lands after him. Friðleifr's son was called Fróði. He took the kingship after his father at the time when Augustus the emperor established peace over the whole world. At that time Christ was born. And because Fróði was the most powerful of all kings in the Northern lands, the peace was named after him throughout all the Danish-speaking lands, and the Norwegians call it Fróði's Peace. No man harmed another, even if he came upon his father's slayer or his brother's slayer, free or bound. There was then also no thief or robber, so that a gold ring lay for a long time on Jalangrsheiðr. King Fróði went on a visit to Svíþjóð [Sweden] to the king who is named Fjölnir. There he bought two slave-women, who were called Fenja and Menja. They were big and strong. At that time two millstones were found in Danmörk so large that no one was strong enough to turn them. And this property went with the mill, that whatever the one grinding asked for was ground out on the mill. That mill was called Grótti. The man who gave King Fróði the mill is named Hengikjöptr. King Fróði had the slave-women led to the mill and bade them grind gold and peace and happiness for Fróði. Then he gave them no longer rest or sleep than while the cuckoo was silent or a song could be spoken. It is said that they then spoke the poem that is called Gróttasöngr. And before the poem was ended, they ground an army against Fróði, so that in that night there came the sea-king who was called Mýsingr, and he killed Fróði and took great plunder there. Then Fróði's Peace came to an end. Mýsingr took Grótti with him, and Fenja and Menja too, and bade them grind salt. He bade them grind longer.
